newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada banks seen pressured by rising U.S. rates.
newsitem.headline: Canada banks seen pressured by rising U.S. rates.

text.p: Canadian bank profits are expected to be hurt by rising U.S. interest rates, which have dampened equity markets, mutual funds and the banks' key brokerage business, analysts said.
They said that with a sustained rise in U.S. rates, Canada's big six banks would be unable to match their solid 21 percent earnings growth in fiscal 1996 ended October 31.
The six banks topped C$6 billion in 1996 earnings, for their third straight year of record profits.

"If interest rates rise, then the demand and the rate of growth in some of our key credit aggregates such as mortgages and consumer credit and business loans will become weaker," said Harry Hassanwalia, deputy chief economist at Royal Bank of Canada.
In this year's first quarter ended January 31, bank earnings rose 12.5 percent, propelled by growing loan demand amid an improving economy, and surging securities markets.
Canada's banks dominate the Canadian securities industry through their ownership of most major brokerages.
Last week's U.S. rate rise took the steam out of stock markets and increased pressure on Canada's central bank to raise its own rates, threatening Canada's modest economic growth.

"Bank earnings are generally becoming more market-driven," said Nigel Heath of Dominion Bond Rating Service. "When the stock market is booming, bank earnings are booming as investment banking becomes a much greater part of earnings."
Heath said losses in equity markets and declining retail interest in mutual funds and stocks would hurt the securities businesses that provided the biggest growth for banks last year.
"It will affect the brokerage earnings," Heath said. "Overall I expect earnings to improve, but not at the pace that we've seen in 1996."

The Toronto Stock Exchange -- Canada's biggest equity market -- has fallen eight of the nine sessions since the Fed hike. The exchange's bank index has fallen 38.52 points to 429.99 in that period, with shares of Royal Bank, Canada's largest, down by 5.30 to 53.85.
Royal Bank's Hassanwalia noted that corporate loans were also down and that rising interest rates would hurt the reviving consumer loan and mortgages businesses.
"The rise in interest rates, if it's sustained, then I think the categories of credit that will really slow down are household, consumer credit and mortgages."
Hassanwalia said that the banks, however, could see a rise in corporate financing as capital markets got more expensive.
